George Washington. The commander-in-chief of the Continental Army and the central figure of the American Revolution, often called the Father of His Country. A Virginia planter turned soldier, he held the revolutionary cause together through eight years of defeat, starvation, and hardship, outlasting British superiority through strategic patience and unwavering resolve.

Washington led the Continental Army from 1775 to 1783, holding together a ragtag force against the world's premier military power through strategic brilliance and force of personality. He achieved a stunning victory at Trenton in December of 1776 by crossing the ice-choked Delaware River in a surprise dawn attack, turning the tide of morale after months of devastating defeats.

He endured the brutal winter of 1777 and 1778 at Valley Forge in Pennsylvania, where his army nearly froze and starved. He held the force together through sheer leadership, preventing mutiny and collapse. Throughout the war, he adopted a Fabian strategy of avoiding decisive battle except when odds were favorable, preserving his army as the revolution's moral center even in strategic retreat.

His greatest military achievement was coordinating with French forces under Rochambeau at Yorktown in 1781 to trap British General Cornwallis's army, securing the final decisive victory of the war.

But Washington's true greatness lay in what he did after winning. He voluntarily relinquished command in 1783 and returned to private life, shocking European monarchies accustomed to generals seizing power. This choice proved the revolution was genuine.

He presided over the Constitutional Convention of 1787, lending his authority to the new federal framework and breaking deadlocks through his silent but formidable presence. He then served as the nation's first president from 1789 to 1797, setting critical precedents: the two-term tradition, cabinet government, the cabinet's advisory role, and the principle of executive restraint. He established diplomatic credibility for the fledgling republic, navigating between British and French interests while maintaining neutrality during the wars of the French Revolution.

His voluntary relinquishment of power twice—after the revolution and after two terms as president—became the foundational myth of American republicanism: the general who could have been king but chose not to be. This made him inseparable from the nation itself.
